# Why Does Changing Fire Weather Matter?

The devastating 2019–20 Australian bushfire season raised an important question: how is climate change affecting the likelihood of extreme fire-weather conditions?

For local governments and emergency management professionals, this is more than a scientific question. Understanding how climate risk changes can help inform long-term preparedness and resilience planning.

In this post, I summarise research by van Oldenborgh et al. (2021) on the influence of anthropogenic climate change on extreme fire-weather risk in southeastern Australia.

## What Did the Research Find?

The study found that anthropogenic climate change increased the likelihood of extreme fire-weather conditions. Climate-model results estimated that an event with a Fire Weather Index (FWI) as high as that observed in 2019–20 was approximately 80% more likely than in the early twentieth-century climate. The conservative lower bound was approximately 30%.
The estimated change in risk is summarised in @fig-fwi-risk. The comparison shows why historical fire-weather probabilities may no longer provide a sufficient guide to future preparedness.


![Estimated relative likelihood of an extreme fire-weather event across climate scenarios. The early twentieth-century climate is the baseline.](figure1.png){#fig-fwi-risk}
The present-climate estimate is approximately 1.8 times the baseline likelihood, with a conservative lower bound of about a 30% increase. Under a 2°C warmer climate, the estimated likelihood is approximately eight times the baseline, with a lower bound of about four times. The future estimate is uncertain because only two climate models were available for that analysis.
